title: The Afternoon Brief: FIFA's African bloc cracks as Lakers deal sets a record
dek: Six Arab federations declared full backing for Gianni Infantino even as Isha Johansen became the first prominent African football figure to call for his resignation, while the Lakers' agreed $12.5 billion sale and a wave of preseason and transfer news filled out a busy Thursday.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: African football's united front behind Infantino is fracturing in public for the first time, even as six Arab federations moved to shore up his position ahead of the 2027 election.
bottom_line: Thursday's central development was FIFA's governance fight splitting further into the open, with Isha Johansen becoming the first prominent African football figure to call for Infantino's resignation even as six Arab federations declared full support for him hours later. The Lakers' agreed $12.5 billion sale to Josh Kushner and Bob Iger, still pending NBA board approval in September, set a record price for a professional sports franchise. Russell Westbrook's retirement closed out an 18-year career as the NBA's all-time triple-double leader. The reporting establishes the positions taken by federations and officials but does not resolve how the vote balance shifts ahead of any 2027 FIFA challenge. Coming checkpoints include the NBA board of governors' September meeting, Pearsall's recovery progress, and this weekend's preseason returns for Watson and Allen.
body: The day's central story is FIFA's governance fight, and it moved on two fronts at once. Isha Johansen, a former FIFA Council member and ex-president of the Sierra Leone Football Association, publicly called on Gianni Infantino to resign over the collapsed FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal, becoming the first prominent African football figure to break from the continental bloc that has shielded him from pressure. Hours later, six Arab federations, Morocco, Qatar, Egypt, Mauritania, Lebanon and Sudan, declared their full support and confidence in Infantino, a counterweight that arrived the same day Johansen's dissent became public.

The two threads sit in tension. UEFA, CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation have jointly called the withdrawn $20 billion World Cup privatization plan a fundamental breach of trust, and England, Wales and Ireland have withdrawn support for Infantino's 2027 reelection bid. CAF's executive committee remains officially unified behind him, and Motsepe has defended him on loyalty grounds, but Johansen's statement is the first crack in that unity, invoking Infantino's own 2021 advice to her to step down for the good of football and turning it back on him.

Away from FIFA, the day's other headline number was the Lakers. Mark Walter has agreed to sell the franchise to a group led by Josh Kushner and Bob Iger for $12.5 billion, a record price for a professional sports franchise, roughly ten months after Walter took controlling interest at a valuation near $10 billion. The sale is agreed but not closed; it needs approval from the NBA board of governors, which next meets in September.

The rest of the day was a mix of transactions and injury updates. Russell Westbrook announced his retirement after 18 seasons, closing his career as the NBA's all-time triple-double leader with 209, fourteenth on the scoring list and fifth in assists. In soccer, Manchester City completed the signing of goalkeeper Geronimo Rulli from Marseille on a two-year deal to back up Gianluigi Donnarumma, Inter Milan advanced talks with Tottenham for full-back Djed Spence in a deal worth a minimum of 25.6 million pounds, and Celta Vigo's La Liga opener was postponed after a fungal outbreak on the Balaidos pitch, a decision Osasuna disputed as overriding a prior agreement between the clubs. In the NFL, Carolina agreed a one-year deal with tight end Darren Waller, the 49ers' Ricky Pearsall had PCL surgery targeting a nine-month recovery toward the 2027 season, and preseason news included Deshaun Watson named the Browns' starter against Chicago, Josh Allen and Buffalo's starters set to play the first game at the new Highmark Stadium, Carson Beck held out of Arizona's game against Las Vegas with a rib injury team sources called not serious, and a fight between Eagles teammates Moro Ojomo and Fred Johnson at Thursday's practice that required staff intervention. In swimming, Katie Ledecky won the 1,500 freestyle at the Pan Pacific Championships in 15:36.09, her closest finish in the event in 13 years, and a U.S. quartet lowered the mixed medley relay world record to 3:36.70. The desk also reported the death of former boxer Prichard Colon at 33, nearly 11 years after a traumatic brain injury sustained in a 2015 fight, and continued coverage of Matt Hasselbeck's participation in a Boston University study seeking the first living diagnosis of CTE.

The reporting on the FIFA situation lays out positions and statements clearly but does not establish how the balance of votes will move before any 2027 challenge takes shape; that remains an open question the stories do not resolve. The Pearsall and Beck items are grounded in team and source characterizations of injury severity, not medical predictions of outcome.

What to watch in the coming days: whether other African football federations follow Johansen's lead or whether the Arab federations' declaration holds the continental coalition together; the NBA board of governors' September meeting on the Lakers sale; Pearsall's recovery timeline and the 49ers' receiver depth for the rest of 2026; Beck's availability after his rib injury; and how Watson and Allen perform in their preseason returns to game action this weekend.
